solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Prison dispute heard in courtyard

indicators.note: something heard is taken by ear, so the sound of the words counts rather than their spelling

blocks.note: quod is old British slang for a jail
a wrangle is a long noisy argument; its silent W drops out in speech

explanation.surface: An argument among inmates can be overheard out in the prison yard.
explanation.walkthrough: Said together, QUOD WRANGLE sounds just like QUADRANGLE. Quod is dated British slang for prison, which many solvers will not know.
explanation.definitionFit: A quadrangle is an enclosed four-sided yard surrounded by buildings, as in a college or school.

clue.text: Subject to vitality, gains experience

blocks.note: under someone's control means subject to it
go is energy or get-up-and-go

explanation.surface: Someone full of energy picks up experience as they go along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gains experience' reads as a single phrase, but the wordplay gains, or yields, the verb 'experience' as definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo something is to go through or suffer it, the verb sense of living through an event.

clue.text: Party craving senior member

blocks.note: a do is an informal party
a yen is a longing

explanation.surface: A political party hungry for an experienced elder statesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests politics, but here it is just a social do.
explanation.definitionFit: A doyen is the most respected or longest-serving person of a group or profession.

clue.text: Insults workers holding very loud unending argument

indicators.note: with no ending the word loses its final letter
to hold is to have within one's grasp, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: worker ants: crossword shorthand for workers
fortissimo in musical notation
a row is a quarrel; its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Staff insult each other during a noisy argument that never ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workers' as ants is a crossword staple; FF, the fortissimo marking, is the setter's 'very loud'.
explanation.definitionFit: Affronts are open insults or slights to someone's dignity, used here as a plural noun or verb.

clue.text: Home patch for the Avon lady?

definitions.text: Home patch for the Avon lady?

blocks.clueFragment: Home patch for the Avon lady?
blocks.note: surface reading: the sales territory of a door-to-door cosmetics saleswoman from Avon
setter's reading: a woman living by the River Avon, or in the former county of Avon, whose home is an English county

explanation.walkthrough: Avon cosmetics are sold door to door by 'Avon ladies' with their own patch. But Avon was also a county (1974-96) carved largely from GLOUCESTERSHIRE, a county in western England through which the Avon flows.
explanation.definitionFit: A county is a home region, the patch where a resident of the Avon area lives.

clue.text: Number of personnel eventually included

indicators.note: what is included sits inside other words, so the letters lie within the run of text

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A headcount of staff that finally included everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles personnEL EVENtually.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven is a cardinal number, one more than ten, so it is an instance of the general word.

clue.text: Resistance units — I see thousands

blocks.note: 'oh, I see' is an exclamation of understanding
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so several are Ms

explanation.surface: A wartime resistance group realises it has thousands of members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resistance' hints at partisans, but it is the electrical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: The ohm is the standard physics measure of electrical resistance, named after Georg Ohm.

clue.text: Fruit cultivated near Quito

indicators.note: cultivated ground is worked over and turned, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Fruit grown on farms close to Ecuador's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Quito suggests South America, but the fruit actually comes from Jamaica.
explanation.definitionFit: An ortanique is a Jamaican citrus hybrid of orange and tangerine, a specific kind of fruit.

clue.text: Former President from island meeting endless hold-up

indicators.note: without an end, the word loses its last letter
one thing meeting another puts them side by side, end to end

blocks.note: the Isle of Man
a delay is a hold-up; the final letter goes

explanation.surface: A one-time head of state arriving from an island meets a long delay.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man lies between Britain and Ireland; MAN is the stock island in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson Mandela was South Africa's first democratically elected head of state, serving 1994 to 1999.

clue.text: Unknown tot turning back at end of war

indicators.note: turning to face backwards makes the letters read from right to left

blocks.note: algebra's unknowns are x, y and z
to tot up is to add

explanation.surface: A small child of no name turns round as the war ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' looks like a child, but it is the verb to tot up. The Normandy landings of June 1944 marked the beginning of the end of the war.
explanation.definitionFit: D-Day, the Allied invasion of Normandy, began the final campaign that brought the European war to a close.

clue.text: Like the Medici family’s chocolate-covered biscuit

blocks.note: first meaning: from Florence, the city the Medici ruled
second meaning: a thin nut-and-fruit biscuit coated with chocolate

explanation.surface: The Medici household's favourite chocolate biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes one phrase of two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the adjective for things from Florence and also the name of a crisp nutty biscuit backed with chocolate.

clue.text: Ella goes and breaks collarbone on rough ride

definitions.note: the horse that gives the ride, not the ride itself

indicators.note: what goes is taken away, so those letters are removed
something broken is smashed apart and its parts rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; these letters leave the longer word

explanation.surface: A girl called Ella fractures her collarbone after being thrown on a bumpy ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing E, L, L and A from COLLARBONE leaves CORBON, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A bronco is an untamed bucking horse, whose rider is in for a rough and violent journey.

clue.text: Freed from sin, is inclined to enter church that’s deserted

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: Church of England
to lean is to be inclined
the abbreviation for deserted

explanation.surface: Someone absolved of sin feels drawn to an abandoned church.
explanation.walkthrough: CE is the abbreviation for the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: To be cleansed in the religious sense is to be purified, washed clean of guilt and wrongdoing.

clue.text: Old philosopher inside an emergency call box

indicators.note: what is inside sits within something else, so one piece is placed in the other

blocks.note: the Morse distress signal
a crate is a wooden box

explanation.surface: An ancient thinker stuck in a phone box for emergencies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call box' suggests a telephone kiosk, but the phrase splits: the call is the distress signal and the box goes into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Socrates was the Athenian thinker of the fifth century BC, teacher of Plato, an ancient philosopher.

clue.text: Jo, in new sarong, has hot Indian dish

indicators.note: something made new is remade, so the letters take a fresh order
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A woman in a new sarong eats a spicy curry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jo' looks like the subject of the sentence, but she is just two letters to be placed inside the rearranged garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Rogan josh is a Kashmiri lamb curry with a rich red sauce, a dish of Indian cooking.

clue.text: Landing-stage is vital, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the word is identified by how it is said

blocks.note: key means essential or crucial

explanation.surface: Someone reports that the jetty is essential.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words are pronounced identically despite the different spellings.
explanation.definitionFit: A quay is a stone or wooden platform where boats moor and load, a landing place.

clue.text: One who goes to bed to work

definitions.text: One who goes to bed to work

blocks.clueFragment: One who goes to bed to work
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who sleeps on the job or works from their bed
setter's reading: a flower bed, where a person digging and planting does their work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed' suggests sleep; it is the plot of soil where flowers grow.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who tends plants spends the working day at flower beds, digging, weeding and planting.

clue.text: Tailless diver comes back to composer

indicators.note: with no tail, the word loses its final letter
coming back means travelling the other way, so the letters read right to left

blocks.note: a grebe is a diving waterbird; its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A diver who has lost a fin returns to visit a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diver' suggests a person, but it is the bird. Alban Berg was an Austrian composer of the Second Viennese School.
explanation.definitionFit: Alban Berg wrote the operas Wozzeck and Lulu, making him a twentieth-century composer.

clue.text: Demanding leave to absorb information

indicators.note: absorbing takes something in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to exit is to leave
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Insisting on time off so as to take in the facts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demanding' looks like a verb, but it is the adjective, and 'leave' is a verb, not time off.
explanation.definitionFit: Exigent describes something pressing or requiring much effort, an adjective close to exacting.

clue.text: Very dry wicket perhaps upset the stands

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are turned to read the other way

blocks.note: sere means withered and parched
a wicket gate is a small gate, so a wicket is an example of one

explanation.surface: A parched cricket pitch annoys the crowd in the grandstands.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture misleads: the wicket is a small gate, and the stands are furniture, not seating. In cricket the wicket is the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: An étagère is a piece of furniture with open shelves for displaying ornaments, a kind of display stand.

clue.text: Bean-cheese and pheasant, say. No good

indicators.note: saying no to something refuses it, so those letters are left out

blocks.note: a Dutch cheese
pheasant is an example of game bird
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A menu item: bean and cheese, with pheasant, judged poor.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'Bean-cheese' welds definition to wordplay to suggest a food.
explanation.definitionFit: Edamame are young green soya beans in the pod, served boiled and salted in Japanese cooking.

clue.text: King in a French shack, not harmed

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: un is French for a
a hut is a shack
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch sheltering in a cabin in France escapes injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A French' means the French word for a, a common crossword device; the king is R from Latin rex.
explanation.definitionFit: Unhurt means without injury, an adjective equivalent to the phrase for being left unharmed.

clue.text: Spoils Warwickshire opener’s time at the crease

indicators.note: an opener begins things, so only the start of the word is kept

blocks.note: the initial of the county name
in cricket a batter's innings is the spell at the crease

explanation.surface: A county batter's long stay at the wicket spoils the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' looks like a verb but is the noun for loot. Warwickshire is an English county cricket team; the crease is where the batter stands.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoils are prizes or loot taken by a victor, and winnings are money or prizes gained.

clue.text: Composer, having drunk vodka, runs inside

indicators.note: what is inside sits within something else, so one piece goes into another
a drunk person staggers about, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A musician who has had too much vodka dashes indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' reads as the past tense of drink, but it means intoxicated and scrambles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonín Dvořák was the Czech composer of the New World Symphony.

clue.text: The church keys?

blocks.note: surface reading: the keys that unlock the church door
setter's reading: the keyboard of the big instrument played in church

explanation.walkthrough: 'Keys' suggests locks, but it means a keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: The pipe instrument played at services is the church's keyboard instrument par excellence.

clue.text: Spin doctor live, on tour

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political spin doctor performing live on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin doctor' looks like one phrase, a press adviser, but it splits into definition and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A revolution is one complete turn around an axis, the rotating motion of a wheel.

clue.text: Eat snacks during the day, mostly in Austrian city

indicators.note: mostly means not entirely, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: to graze is to nibble small bites throughout the day

explanation.surface: Someone nibbling between meals while visiting a city in Austria.
explanation.walkthrough: Graze as a verb describes snacking instead of eating proper meals.
explanation.definitionFit: Graz is the capital of Styria and the second largest urban centre in Austria.

clue.text: State of posh hat that’s returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: U means upper-class, in the old U and non-U usage
taken as written

explanation.surface: The condition of a smart hat that was sent back to the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State of' suggests a condition, but the state is American.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah is one of the fifty constituent states of the USA, with Salt Lake City as capital.

clue.text: Shorten bet about literary family

indicators.note: about can mean around or roughly, so the letters are turned around into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bookmaker cuts the odds on a famous writing family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shorten bet' sounds like betting jargon for cutting odds.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë were sisters who all wrote celebrated novels, a family of writers.
